lead: Today the Syriac Churches remember Mar Behnam, his sister Sarah and the Forty Martyrs. The readings give two faces of Christian witness. In Thessalonica it is a quiet life of love, honest work and good standing with neighbours. In Matthew it is open confession before those who can kill the body. Jesus says “do not be afraid” because the Father knows the fall of every sparrow.

r.h: Taught by God to love one another
set: First Thessalonians is very probably the oldest surviving Christian writing, from about AD 50 or 51. Paul had to leave this young church in Macedonia in a hurry, and he writes with joy at the good report he has received. In chapter 4 he turns to how they should live. Some of them may have been neglecting ordinary work; he returns to this in 2 Thessalonians 3:6–12.
str: vv. 9–10a: on love: you have been taught by God, and you already practise it.
v. 10b: do so more and more.
vv. 11–12: live quietly, work, and depend on no one.
kw: love of the brothers and sisters
In the Greek world this word meant love between children of one family. Christians used it for the new family of faith.
This word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It recalls the promises of Isaiah 54:13 and Jeremiah 31:33–34, that in the new age God himself would teach his people.
Paul makes a small paradox. The verb “aspire” means to pursue honour eagerly. Here the honour to be pursued is quietness.
vv: you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another;
The law of love is written within them by the Spirit. Paul does not need to teach it; he only needs to remind them.
to aspire to live quietly, to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we directed you,
Paul himself worked night and day so as not to burden anyone (2:9). Greek society of his time often despised manual work. Here it becomes part of a Christian witness.
so that you may behave properly toward outsiders and be dependent on no one.
Love looks outward too: the neighbour who does not share the faith sees how Christians live.
ch: The Catechism says that work honours the Creator's gifts and that it can be a means of holiness, united to Christ the carpenter of Nazareth (CCC 2427). Love is the first gift of the Spirit, which no one can give himself. The martyrs we remember today did not begin with a great moment. They began, as we do, with daily faithfulness.

set: This passage belongs to the second of Jesus' five great discourses in Matthew, in which he sends out the Twelve (Matthew 10). He has just warned them of courts, floggings and hatred (10:17–25). Now the tone changes. Three times he says that they are not to fear (vv. 26, 28, 31). Matthew's first readers probably knew from experience what this meant.
str: vv. 26–27: do not fear, because the truth will come out: proclaim it.
v. 28: do not fear those who can only kill the body.
vv. 29–31: do not fear, for the Father cares even for sparrows.
vv. 32–33: acknowledge Jesus, and he will acknowledge you.
kw: From the Hebrew name for the valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, a place remembered for child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31; 2 Kings 23:10). It became an image of final ruin.
A small copper coin of little value. Two sparrows for one such coin: the cheapest living thing in the market.
To say the same thing, to declare openly, as one does in a court. It is the word for confession of faith.
vv: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
The one to be feared is God, not the devil. This is reverence, not terror, since the next verse speaks of this same God as “your Father”. Fear of God frees a person from every other fear.
Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
Jesus does not promise that the sparrow will not fall. He promises that it will not fall alone. This is a word for martyrs.
“Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven;
Our confession on earth and Christ's confession before the Father are joined. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473).
ch: The Catechism draws on verses like these when it teaches that God's care reaches the smallest things (CCC 302–305), and that Jesus' warnings about Gehenna are a call to responsibility and conversion (CCC 1034, 1036). The Church has always kept the memory of her martyrs, and she has read this chapter as being fulfilled in them.

rite: The tradition of the Syriac Churches tells that Mar Behnam and Sarah were children of a Persian ruler in the fourth century, that Behnam came to faith through the monk Mar Mattai, that Sarah was healed and baptised, and that they were put to death with forty companions. The story as we have it is partly legendary, and its details cannot be checked. What is certain is the long love of the Syriac faithful for these martyrs, witnessed by the ancient monastery that bears Mar Behnam's name near Mosul in northern Iraq. Christians of that land have suffered greatly in our own time, and today's Gospel may lead us to pray for them at the Holy Qurbono.
study: Which is harder for me today: the quiet faithfulness Paul describes, or open witness before others?
What fear is holding me back from acknowledging Christ, and what does the image of the sparrow say to it?
